records.our_prose: Field corn, also called dent corn, is a tall grass grown not for fresh eating but for the hard, dry grain inside the ear. You let the ears ripen and dry right on the stalk, then shell off the kernels to grind into cornmeal, grits, or masa for tortillas, or to feed to livestock and poultry. Old open-pollinated types like John Haulk and Cocke's Prolific can tower up to 15 feet, while modern grain hybrids are shorter and faster. Like all corn it is pollinated by wind, so you plant it in a square block of short rows, not a single line, so the tassels can dust the silks and fill the ears. One important warning: field corn pollen will drift into nearby sweet corn or popcorn and ruin them, turning sweet kernels starchy and keeping popcorn from popping, so keep them at least 300 feet apart or time your plantings so they tassel about two weeks apart.
records.source_context: As mentioned previously, because sweet corn is wind pollinated, quality is best if the stands are isolated from field corn, popcorn, and ornamental corn, as well as from other types of sweet corn. Isolation, in this sense, means either planting the crops at least 300 feet apart, or staggering plantings so that there is a 10 to 14 day difference in maturity between crops.

records.our_prose: Field corn is a warm-season crop here, sown once the soil reaches 60°F, roughly two weeks after the last spring frost. Season length is the binding constraint for a 95-to-120-day dent: favor early grain varieties, sow at the first warm soil, and in the shortest zones pick at hard dent and cure under cover, since the crop may not fully field-dry before frost.

records.source_context: If the soil becomes too dry, their growth may be seriously limited. Most vegetable crops require 1 inch of water per week for optimum pro- duction. If your area does not receive this amount of rainfall each week during the growing season, you will need to irrigate your garden using overhead sprinklers, soaker hoses, drip tape or hand watering.
